methodological_rigor.justification: A 509-patient real-world multicenter cohort (six Austrian centers, 2015-2022) with rigorous statistical handling: propensity-score IPTW with 25 multiple-imputation datasets for missing covariates, SMD <0.20 threshold for balance, flexible parametric survival models with restricted cubic splines for time-dependent effects, restricted mean survival time (RMST) analysis for non-proportional hazards, and formal Schoenfeld-residual testing. A sensitivity analysis censoring at next-line initiation addresses treatment cross-over confounding. Limitations are retrospective design, no central response review, non-standardized restaging, and missing safety/toxicity data due to non-standardized documentation.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Propensity-score-balanced retrospective multicenter cohort maps to Oxford LoE 2b. Clinical relevance is substantial: the study confirms in real-world practice the SUNLIGHT-trial finding that FTD-TPI+bevacizumab outperforms FTD-TPI or regorafenib in pretreated mCRC, and importantly extends the finding across KRAS/KRASG12 molecular subgroups where prior evidence was mixed. The BRAFV600E subgroup finding (no benefit and numerical trend toward inferiority, interaction P=0.020) is clinically actionable for treatment selection.

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE is the applicable standard for an observational cohort. The manuscript covers most STROBE items: setting, participants, variables, statistical methods, confounding handling via IPTW, missing-data management via multiple imputation, sensitivity analyses, and explicit discussion of limitations. Propensity-score diagnostics (SMD assessment, Supplementary Figures/Tables) are provided. Weaknesses: no explicit STROBE checklist reference, and data availability is limited to the supplementary materials with no deposition of de-identified patient-level data or analysis code.

novelty_literature.justification: The study extends the SUNLIGHT trial (FTD-TPI+bevacizumab vs FTD-TPI) to a broader real-world population including a comparator arm (regorafenib) and systematically evaluates molecular subgroups (KRAS, KRASG12, BRAFV600E, TP53, PIK3CA, NRAS). A similar real-world comparison in Japanese administrative data was previously reported (Kagawa 2023), so the contribution is incremental and confirmatory rather than first-in-class. The BRAFV600E subgroup finding and the TP53-mutant hypothesis-generating observation add novel translational insights.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well-organized with clear exposition of cohort, methods, unadjusted vs IPTW-adjusted results, time-dependent analyses, and molecular subgroups. Tables are detailed and informative. Limitations are explicitly addressed (retrospective design, response assessment, crossover, residual confounding, absence of toxicity data). Minor issues: some table formatting (Table 1) is compressed in the markdown rendering and the abstract's three bullet points are duplicated verbatim below.

key_strengths: Large real-world multicenter cohort (n=509 across six Austrian centers) with rigorous propensity-score IPTW methodology and appropriate handling of non-proportional hazards via flexible parametric models and RMST
Systematic molecular-subgroup analysis addressing the previously uncertain KRASG12 question, finding consistent benefit of FTD-TPI+bevacizumab (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.36-0.93)
Formal sensitivity analysis censoring at next-line initiation addresses treatment crossover confounding in OS estimates
Clinically relevant BRAFV600E interaction finding (P=0.020) provides a testable subgroup hypothesis
Transparent discussion of limitations and clear framing of real-world vs trial population differences
key_concerns: Retrospective design with no central radiology review and non-standardized restaging schedules across centers
Significant treatment crossover between arms may attenuate OS differences even with sensitivity analysis
Systematic safety/toxicity data not available due to non-standardized reporting across centers
Incremental/confirmatory novelty relative to SUNLIGHT and prior real-world Japanese data (Kagawa 2023)
PIK3CA and TP53 analyses have high missingness (67% and 72% respectively), limiting interpretability of subgroup results
No data or code sharing statement
chief_reviewer.rationale: A methodologically strong real-world comparative-effectiveness study with rigorous causal-inference methods and a clinically actionable molecular-subgroup finding; tier 2 (e.g., ESMO Open, Annals of Oncology, European Journal of Cancer) is plausible at its highest, with tier 1 precluded by the observational design and incremental advance over SUNLIGHT.
